front: Resolution of metre rule, vernier, micrometer?
Why time 20 oscillations instead of one?
back: Reaction-time uncertainty is shared over 20, cutting the percentage uncertainty.

front: How are ammeters and voltmeters connected?
back: Ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel.
Reading a scale at an angle; avoid by viewing at eye level, perpendicular to the scale.

front: Three things a risk assessment covers?

back: The smallest change in a quantity that the instrument can detect — e.g. the smallest scale division.

front: Default uncertainty of a single reading on an analogue vs a digital instrument?
back: Analogue scale: ± half the smallest division. Digital display: ± one unit of the last digit.

front: What is a **zero error**, and how do you deal with it?
back: A non-zero reading when the true value is zero (e.g. a micrometer that reads 0.02 mm when closed). It is a systematic error: subtract it from every reading.

front: How do you estimate the uncertainty from several repeated readings?
back: Take the mean as the value and use half the range, $\dfrac{\text{max} - \text{min}}{2}$, as the absolute uncertainty.
Averaging reduces the effect of random errors and makes anomalous readings easy to spot. It does **not** remove systematic errors.

front: Where should you start and stop timing a pendulum, and why?
back: At the equilibrium position, marked with a fiducial marker: the bob moves fastest there, so the moment it passes is the most precisely judged.

front: What is wrong with timing a single oscillation with a stopwatch?
back: Human reaction time (~0.1–0.2 s) is large compared with one period, so the percentage uncertainty is huge. Time 10–20 oscillations and divide.

front: How should the diameter of a thin wire be measured?
back: With a micrometer, at several points along the wire and in perpendicular directions, then averaged; check the zero reading first.

front: How does a light gate give a speed?
back: It times how long a card of known length interrupts the beam: $v = \dfrac{\text{card length}}{\text{time}}$ — no reaction-time error.
Independent: the one you deliberately change. Dependent: the one you measure in response. Control: those kept constant so the test is fair.

front: How should you choose the values of the independent variable?
back: Use at least five (ideally more) values spread evenly over as wide a range as practical, with repeats, so a trend and any curvature are clear.

front: How do you get a reliable temperature reading of a liquid?
back: Stir it, wait for the thermometer to reach thermal equilibrium, and read the scale at eye level (avoiding parallax).

front: What happens if an ammeter is connected in parallel with a component?
back: Its very low resistance short-circuits the component: a large current flows through the ammeter, giving a wrong reading and possibly damaging it.
